analysis.one_liner: Requires regular high-tech inspections and leak checks on gas pipelines in populated areas and doubles penalties for safety violations.
analysis.headline: The pipeline safety bill, introduced with bipartisan support after a deadly New Jersey explosion, never got a vote — it sat in two House committees until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After a 1994 gas pipeline explosion in the Durham Woods neighborhood of Edison, New Jersey, this bill would have required pipeline companies to run internal inspection tools through gas pipelines in dense neighborhoods at least every seven years, walk or fly their lines monthly looking for leaks, and post line markers along rights-of-way. It would have doubled the maximum criminal sentences and civil fines for pipeline safety violations, made it a crime for an excavator to damage a pipeline and not report it, and funded state programs teaching the public about the dangers of digging near gas lines. It also directed federal studies of New Jersey's pipelines and creation of a national pipeline map. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, and go to school near large gas pipelines — especially in crowded suburbs where homes have been built up around pipeline rights-of-way. The bill's requirements would have found corrosion and leaks before they caused explosions, and its public-awareness grants would have warned excavators and residents about the danger of digging near buried lines.

how_it_helps.text: Requires internal inspection of gas pipelines in high-density population areas at least once every seven years using instrumented internal inspection devices — the tools that detect corrosion and wall thinning inside a pipe before it fails.

Requires gas transmission pipeline operators to inspect the surface along their rights-of-way at least monthly for leaks, construction, and other hazards, and to place line markers so people know where buried lines run.

Doubles the maximum criminal sentences for knowing pipeline safety violations (for example, from 5 to 10 years, and from 15 to 30 years for violations causing death) and doubles civil fines, from $25,000 to $50,000 per violation with a $1 million cap.
Makes it a federal crime for someone digging to damage a pipeline and fail to report it promptly to the operator and authorities.

Creates federal grants so states can run public-awareness campaigns about the dangers of excavating near pipelines, and directs a comprehensive national mapping program so pipeline locations are known to state and local governments and the public.

analysis.who_pays: Gas pipeline companies, which would bear the cost of regular internal inspections, monthly right-of-way patrols, markers, and mapping — costs likely passed at least partly to their customers through rates. Construction and excavation contractors would also face new federal criminal liability for damaging a pipeline and staying quiet about it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gas pipeline companies and excavation contractors

drawbacks.text: The inspection mandates are blunt: a fixed seven-year inspection cycle in all high-density areas applies the same rule everywhere rather than letting regulators rank pipelines by actual risk, which can drive spending on low-risk lines — and those costs tend to show up in customers' gas bills.

The new criminal penalty for excavators who damage a pipeline without promptly reporting it exposes contractors and even individual equipment operators to federal prosecution, on top of the doubled criminal sentences for operators.

The bill's grants for public-awareness programs were available only 'to the extent provided in advance in appropriations Acts,' so the safety education component would have depended on future Congresses actually funding it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but modest relative to the harm the bill targeted: the Durham Woods explosion had shown what a corroded gas line in a built-up neighborhood can do. The fixed inspection schedule is less efficient than a purely risk-based approach, and the criminal provisions are sweeping, but the core requirements — periodic internal inspection, monthly patrols, markers, and a national map — are standard safety measures that the industry now operates under in some form. On balance the benefits to people living near pipelines outweighed the compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and one of their subcommittees even held hearings, but neither committee ever voted it out, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Franks of New Jersey introduced the bill on March 3, 1995, joined by 11 cosponsors — 6 Democrats and 5 Republicans, nearly all from the New Jersey delegation.
The House referred it to both the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the Commerce Committee, and it was split between the Surface Transportation and Energy and Power subcommittees.
The Surface Transportation subcommittee held hearings on the bill in March 1995, but no subcommittee or full committee ever voted on it.
The bill's only further action was sponsor introductory remarks read into the record a year later, in March 1996; it never reached the House floor and expired at the end of the 104th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gas pipeline operators came out ahead: they avoided new inspection mandates, doubled fines, and a national mapping requirement for the rest of the 1990s. Residents near gas transmission lines got no added federal protections from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gas pipeline operators, not nearby residents

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican and cosponsored evenly across both parties — 6 Democrats and 5 Republicans — with no party opposing it on record; it simply never advanced in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have required internal inspections every seven years in dense areas, monthly right-of-way patrols, line markers, pipeline mapping, and doubled civil and criminal fines. Pipeline companies' interest in avoiding these costs ran against the safety of people living near their lines, though much of the cost would have been passed to gas customers through rates.

The bill made failing to report damage from excavation a federal crime, but it also funded state public-awareness programs teaching crews the dangers of digging near gas lines. Contractors striking an unmarked pipe are among those endangered by the status quo the bill targeted.
